intro: Two cousins are born a month apart and one walks four months before the other, and the family is sure it means something. A sixteen-year-old takes her first babysitting job and finds a list under a magnet on the refrigerator: phone numbers, an allergy, a bedtime, the rule for the crib. A four-year-old says the dog broke the lamp while holding the ball that broke it. Every one of these is a child development problem, and none of them is solved by loving children. They are solved by knowing what children do at each age, what they cannot yet do, and what keeps them alive while they learn.

The first chapter is the science. You will learn the four domains in which every child grows, physical, cognitive, social and emotional, and the milestones of each as ranges that many children fit, never as deadlines. You will follow a child from the reflexes of a newborn through the will of a toddler, the questions of a preschooler and the friendships of school age, and learn how play does the teaching, how language grows from being talked to, and which few signs mean it is time to talk to a doctor, without shame and without waiting.

The second chapter is the care. You will learn guidance that teaches instead of punishment that frightens: routines, choices, redirection and consequences that fit. You will set up a crib for safe sleep, childproof a home from a crawler's eye level, choose the right car seat for each stage, cut a grape the right way and know the back blows and thrusts if a child chokes anyway. You will gather what a babysitter needs before the parents leave, plan an evening by age, and learn the signs of abuse and neglect and how a concern becomes a report. By the end you will be able to keep a child safe for an evening and explain every rule you followed.
bigQuestion: What does a child need at each stage, and how do you know the difference between a child on their own path and a child who needs help?

timeline.t: Rousseau's Emile argues that childhood is its own stage of life, not a small version of adulthood
Friedrich Froebel opens the first kindergarten in Germany, built on play as the way young children learn
The first White House Conference on Children is held in the United States
Congress creates the U.S. Children's Bureau to study and improve child welfare
Arnold Gesell publishes developmental schedules describing what many children do at each age
Jean Piaget describes how infants build thinking through their senses and actions, including object permanence
Dr. Benjamin Spock's baby and child care book tells parents to trust themselves and respond to their babies
Head Start begins, offering preschool, meals and health care to low-income children
John Bowlby publishes the first volume of Attachment, describing the bond between infant and caregiver
The Child Abuse Prevention and Treatment Act funds state reporting systems and child protection
Federal law guarantees children with disabilities a free public education, later named IDEA
The Back to Sleep campaign begins; infant sleep deaths fall by about half over the following decade

words.d: a skill many children gain within an age range, such as walking between about 9 and 15 months; a range, never a deadline
movements using the large muscles: rolling, sitting, crawling, walking, running
small movements of the hands and fingers: the pincer grasp, stacking, scribbling, cutting
the understanding that things exist when out of sight, gained at about 6 to 10 months
the lasting bond between a child and a caregiver who reliably responds to the child's needs
a child's inborn style of reacting: easy, slow to warm up or intense; not a flaw
toddlers playing beside each other without playing together; normal from about 1 to 3
free evaluation and support for children under 3 with developmental delays, provided through each state
everything an adult does to help a child learn how to behave: routines, choices, redirection, fitting consequences
a result set by the adult that is related to the behavior, respectful and reasonable in size
an infant on the back, on a firm flat surface, alone in the crib with nothing else in it, every sleep
a person the law requires to report reasonable suspicion of child abuse or neglect, such as a teacher or child care worker

test.q: In which order do gross motor milestones usually appear?
choices: Walk, sit, roll, head control
Sit, walk, roll, head control
Head control, roll, sit, walk
Roll, head control, walk, sit
test.why: Control develops from head to toe: head, then trunk (rolling and sitting), then legs (standing and walking).

test.q: A parent says their 13-month-old is "late" because she is not walking. Which reply is accurate?
choices: She should be seen by a specialist this week
She is late; most babies walk by 10 months
Girls walk later, so it is fine
Walking alone commonly happens between about 9 and 15 months, so 13 months is within the usual range
test.why: Milestones are ranges. Thirteen months is inside the common walking range, and the order of skills matters more than the date.

test.q: A nine-month-old cries when a stranger picks him up. This most likely shows:
choices: Healthy attachment; stranger anxiety is expected at about 6 to 9 months
A problem with social development
That he was frightened by the stranger
That he has been held too much
test.why: Stranger anxiety is a normal sign that the baby now knows his own caregivers and prefers them.

test.q: A two-year-old holds a banana to her ear and says "hello." This is an example of:
choices: Egocentrism
Symbolic thinking through pretend play
A fine motor milestone
Parallel play
test.why: Using one object to stand for another is symbolic thinking, a normal toddler milestone and the root of pretend play and language.

test.q: Which sign is a clear reason to see a doctor rather than a normal variation?
choices: A 10-month-old who scoots instead of crawling
A 4-year-old who is afraid of dogs
A 2-year-old who has lost words she used to say and does not respond to her name
A 15-month-old who is not yet walking
test.why: Losing a skill and not responding to sound are warning signs. The other three are within normal ranges.

test.q: Which reply best supports a toddler who points and says "dog"?
choices: "Say dog again."
"What color is the dog? What is it doing? What sound does it make?"
"Mm-hm."
"Yes, a big brown dog! He's running."
test.why: Expanding the child's word with more language about the same thing is the most effective everyday way to grow language.

test.q: A 20-month-old refuses to get dressed. Which approach fits the age?
choices: Explain that she will be late for day care
Ask, "Do you want to get dressed?"
Offer, "The green shirt or the yellow one?"
Put her in a time-out until she agrees
test.why: Toddlers need real choices between two acceptable options. Yes-or-no questions invite no, and explanations and time-outs do not work at this age.

test.q: Which is guidance rather than punishment for a preschooler who drew on the wall?
choices: No television for a week
A spanking so she remembers
Sending her to bed without dinner
Having her help wash the wall and moving the markers to a supervised place
test.why: A logical consequence is related to the behavior, respectful and reasonable in size. Unrelated or physical punishments teach fear, not the skill.

test.q: Which crib is set up correctly for a four-month-old's nap?
choices: Firm mattress, fitted sheet, nothing else, baby on her back
Firm mattress, fitted sheet, light blanket, baby on her side
Soft mattress, bumper pads, baby on her back
Firm mattress, fitted sheet, small stuffed animal, baby on her stomach
test.why: Safe sleep is on the back, on a firm flat surface, with nothing else in the sleep space.

test.q: What is the recommended maximum home water heater setting where children live?
test.why: At 120 °F or lower, tap water is far less likely to scald. Water at 140 °F burns skin in seconds.

test.q: A toddler is found with an open bottle of medicine. What is the first call?
choices: The pediatrician's office
The parents
Poison Control, 1-800-222-1222
The pharmacy
test.why: Poison Control gives immediate instructions for the specific substance. Never induce vomiting unless they say to.

test.q: A six-year-old who is 45 inches tall has outgrown her forward-facing harness seat. What comes next?
choices: The adult seat belt alone in the back seat
The front seat with the airbag on
Back to a rear-facing seat
A booster seat until the adult belt fits, usually around 4 feet 9 inches
test.why: After the harness comes the booster, which lifts the child so the lap belt sits on the thighs and the shoulder belt on the shoulder. The belt alone waits until it fits.

test.q: How should hot dogs and grapes be prepared for a two-year-old?
choices: Hot dogs in thin lengthwise strips and grapes quartered lengthwise
Hot dogs in rounds and grapes halved
Both served whole so the child learns to chew
Hot dogs in rounds and grapes whole, with water to wash them down
test.why: Round pieces the size of a small airway are the main food choking hazard. Long thin pieces cannot plug it.

test.q: An infant under one is choking and silent. Which sequence is correct?
choices: Abdominal thrusts, then a finger sweep
Five back blows face down along the forearm, then five chest thrusts with two fingers, repeat, with 911 called
Hold her upside down and shake
Wait for her to cough it out
test.why: Infants get back blows and chest thrusts, not abdominal thrusts. A silent infant has a blocked airway and 911 is called at once.

test.q: A babysitter suspects a child is being abused. What is required before she reports it to the Illinois DCFS hotline?
choices: Photographs and a witness
The parents' permission
A reasonable suspicion based on what she saw or heard; proof is not required
A second incident to confirm the pattern
test.why: Anyone can report a reasonable concern in good faith, and mandated reporters must. Trained investigators decide what happens next.

write.prompt: You are babysitting a 9-month-old and a 4-year-old from 5:30 to 9:30 p.m. Write the plan: the questions you ask before the parents leave, the evening schedule by age, the safe-sleep steps for the baby, and the guidance tool you will use when the 4-year-old refuses bedtime. Explain why each step is there.
tips: Put the steps in time order, with the baby's bottle and bedtime as fixed points
Name the tool for each part: the information sheet, the sleep sack, the transition warning, the two-option choice
State the safety rule behind each step: back to sleep, nothing in the crib, food cut for the age, Poison Control number
Match each activity to the child's stage and say what the child can and cannot do at that age
Check the numbers: ages, times, temperatures and phone numbers must be the standard ones

title: Child Development and Care

chapters.title: The Four Domains
chapters.bigQuestion: How do you tell the difference between a child who is developing on their own schedule and a child who needs help?

story.title: Two Cousins, One Month Apart
story.kicker: Ava walked at ten months and Mateo walked at fourteen, and the family had opinions about what that meant.
paragraphs: Ava and Mateo were born a month apart, in the same hospital on the Southwest Side, to two sisters who lived four blocks from each other. From the first week the family compared them. Who slept through the night first. Who smiled first. Who rolled over first. The comparing was mostly love, but it had an edge to it, and by the time the babies were nine months old the edge had a name: walking.

Ava pulled up on the coffee table at eight months and took her first wobbling steps at ten. Her grandmother filmed it and sent it to everyone. Mateo, at ten months, was a champion crawler. He could cross a room in seconds, climb onto the couch cushions and pull every book off the bottom shelf, but he had no interest in standing. His mother, Rosa, started to worry. Her sister did not help. "Maybe you should have him checked," she said, in the voice that meant she had already decided something was wrong.

Rosa did ask, at Mateo's twelve-month checkup. The pediatrician watched Mateo crawl, watched him pick up a single Cheerio between his thumb and finger, watched him look up when his name was called and babble back a string of sounds that were almost words. Then she said the thing Rosa would repeat for years afterward. "Most children walk somewhere between nine and fifteen months. He is twelve months old, he is strong, he is curious, and he is talking to me. He is right on time. He is just not on Ava's time."

Mateo walked at fourteen months, on a Tuesday, across the kitchen to get a spoon. By the time the cousins were three, nobody could remember which one had walked first, because by then they were both running, both talking in full sentences, and both fighting over the same tricycle. But one of them had a word Ava did not: Mateo said "helicopter" at two and a half, clearly, and used it correctly, and his grandmother filmed that too.

This chapter is about what the pediatrician knew. Development happens in four areas at once, it follows a predictable order, and it happens on a range, not a schedule. Knowing the ranges is what lets a parent, a teacher or a babysitter relax about the things that are normal and notice the few things that are not.
story.think: Rosa's sister and Rosa's pediatrician looked at the same child and saw two different things. What did the pediatrician know that the sister did not, and how would you explain it to a worried parent?

lessons.title: Physical Development
lessons.mainIdea: Physical development runs from head to toe and from the center of the body outward, on a range that is wide but predictable.
reading: Put a four-month-old on her stomach on a blanket and watch. She pushes up on her forearms, lifts her head, holds it steady and looks around. A month earlier her head wobbled. A month from now she may roll over. This is *physical development*: the growth of the body and the child's gaining control over its muscles. It does not happen at random. Control comes first to the head and neck, then the trunk, then the legs. Doctors call this head-to-toe growth. Control also comes first to the center of the body and moves outward: shoulders before hands, hands before fingers.

Big movements that use the large muscles are *gross motor skills*. In the first year they arrive in a fairly fixed order. Many babies hold their head steady at about 2 to 4 months, roll over at about 4 to 6 months, sit without support at about 6 to 9 months, pull up to stand at about 8 to 12 months, and walk alone somewhere between about 9 and 15 months. Some babies crawl at 7 to 10 months; some scoot on their bottoms; some skip crawling entirely and go straight to walking. The order is what matters, not the calendar.

Small movements of the hands and fingers are *fine motor skills*. A newborn's fist closes on your finger by reflex. At about 4 to 6 months a baby rakes at a toy with the whole hand. Between about 9 and 12 months the *pincer grasp* appears: thumb and forefinger together, picking up one piece of cereal. That grasp is the foundation of everything that comes later. Many children scribble at about 15 to 18 months, stack a small tower of blocks at about 2, copy a circle at about 3, and write some letters of their name at about 5.

Every one of those numbers is a range, and the late end of a range is still on time. A child who walks at 10 months is not ahead; a child who walks at 14 months is not behind. The pediatrician's rule in the story is the rule here: watch the order, watch the range, and watch whether the child keeps gaining new skills. A child who stops gaining skills, or loses a skill she had, is the child to ask about.

words.d: the growth of the body and the child's increasing control over its muscles
movements that use the large muscles: rolling, sitting, crawling, walking, running
small movements of the hands and fingers: grasping, stacking, scribbling, buttoning
picking up a small object between the thumb and forefinger, usually appearing at about 9 to 12 months

look.title: About the Later End of the Usual Range
look.cite: Common ranges from pediatric developmental guides; the early end of each range is months sooner, and every child differs
look.prompt: A parent says their 11-month-old is not walking yet. Using the table, what would you tell them, and which skill would you ask whether the child has?

check.q: A baby can sit without support but cannot yet hold a rattle steadily in one hand. Which pattern of physical development explains this?
choices: Control develops from the center of the body outward, so the trunk comes before the hands
The baby is behind and should be seen by a doctor
Sitting is a fine motor skill and grasping is a gross motor skill
Babies develop hands first and trunk last
check.why: Muscle control spreads from the center outward: trunk and shoulders before hands and fingers. Sitting before a steady grasp is the normal order.

check.q: Which of these is a fine motor skill?
choices: Rolling from back to front
Picking up one piece of cereal with thumb and forefinger
Pulling up to stand at the couch
Crawling across the room
check.why: Fine motor skills use the small muscles of the hands and fingers. The pincer grasp is the classic example.

check.q: A 13-month-old crawls fast, pulls to stand, and cruises along furniture but has not walked alone. What is the best response?
choices: Start daily walking practice with a walker to catch up
Assume something is wrong and stop letting the child crawl
Note that 13 months is inside the usual 9 to 15 month range and the child is gaining skills in order
Compare the child to a cousin who walked at 10 months
check.why: Walking alone commonly arrives between about 9 and 15 months. The child is inside the range and following the normal order, which is what matters.

lessons.title: Cognitive Development
lessons.mainIdea: Cognitive development is how a child learns to think, remember, solve problems and understand that the world keeps existing when they cannot see it.
reading: Hide a toy under a blanket in front of a five-month-old and she looks away, as if the toy has stopped existing. Do the same thing in front of a nine-month-old and he pulls the blanket off. Nothing about his eyes changed; his mind did. This is *cognitive development*: the growth of thinking, memory, attention, problem solving and understanding. The nine-month-old has learned *object permanence*, the idea that things go on existing when you cannot see them. It usually shows up somewhere between about 6 and 10 months, and it is why peek-a-boo suddenly becomes the funniest game in the world.

Infants learn through their senses and their movements. A baby who drops a spoon from the high chair forty times is not being difficult. She is running an experiment: every time, it falls, and every time, someone picks it up. That is cause and effect, and she is learning it the only way she can. Toddlers add memory and imitation. A two-year-old who feeds a doll with a spoon is copying something she saw yesterday and holding it in her head, and she is starting to use one thing to stand for another. That is the beginning of symbolic thinking, which is also the beginning of language and pretend play.

Preschoolers, about 3 to 5, think in a way that is powerful and lopsided. They can sort by color, count a small group of objects, follow a three-step direction and tell you what comes next in a familiar story. They also believe the taller glass holds more juice even when they watched you pour the same juice into it, and they assume everyone sees what they see. That last one is called *egocentrism*. It is not selfishness. It is a stage of thinking that most children move past by about 6 or 7, when they begin to reason more like adults, hold rules in their heads and understand another person's point of view.

The principle: children are not small adults with less information. At each stage they think differently, and the job of an adult is to meet the thinking where it is. You do not reason with a two-year-old about why the cup must stay on the table; you move the cup. You do not expect a four-year-old to share without being asked; you set up the turn. Knowing the stage prevents most of the frustration on both sides.

words.d: the growth of thinking, memory, attention, problem solving and understanding
understanding that things go on existing when they are out of sight, usually gained at about 6 to 10 months
the preschool tendency to assume everyone sees and knows what the child sees and knows; a stage, not selfishness

look.title: The Spoon Experiment
look.text: A 10-month-old in a high chair drops her spoon on the floor. Her father picks it up. She drops it again. He picks it up. This happens eleven times. She laughs each time it hits the floor. On the twelfth time he says, sharply, "Stop it," and she cries. Later he tells his sister the baby was being stubborn on purpose.
look.prompt: What was the baby actually learning, and what could the father do instead of taking it personally? Suggest one change that keeps the learning and saves his patience.

check.q: A seven-month-old cries when his mother leaves the room, even though she was gone only a moment. Which cognitive change makes this new?
choices: Egocentrism, because he thinks she left to upset him
Symbolic thinking, because he imagines her at work
Cause and effect, because he learned crying brings her back
Object permanence, because he now knows she still exists somewhere and wants her back
check.why: Once a baby understands object permanence, at about 6 to 10 months, an absent parent is a parent who exists somewhere else, and the baby protests.

check.q: A four-year-old insists his cup has less juice because it is wider, even though he watched it being poured from the same bottle as his sister's. What is the best explanation?
choices: Preschoolers judge by how things look and do not yet reason about amount staying the same
He is lying to get more juice
He has a vision problem and cannot see the levels
He is behind and should already understand this at four
check.why: Preschool thinking is tied to appearance. Understanding that amount stays the same when the shape changes usually comes at about 6 or 7.

check.q: A two-year-old picks up a block, holds it to her ear and says "Hello?" What does this show?
choices: She is confused about what a block is
She is using one thing to stand for another, the start of symbolic thinking
She is showing egocentrism
She has not yet developed object permanence
check.why: Using a block as a phone is pretend play, and pretend play is symbolic thinking: letting one thing represent another. It is a normal toddler milestone.

lessons.title: Social and Emotional Growth
lessons.mainIdea: Social and emotional development begins with attachment to a caregiver who responds, and grows into the ability to name feelings, wait, share and make friends.
reading: A newborn cries. Someone comes, picks her up, feeds her or changes her or simply holds her. It happens a hundred times a week. Each time, without any words, the baby learns something: when I need help, help comes. That lesson, repeated for months, builds *attachment*, the deep bond between a child and the person who cares for her. It is the foundation of *social development*, learning to relate to other people, and *emotional development*, learning to feel, understand and manage feelings. A baby whose needs are met reliably learns to trust. A baby who is left to cry for long stretches learns that the world does not answer.

Attachment has visible milestones. Many babies smile at a face by about 2 months. By about 6 to 9 months many show stranger anxiety, going quiet or crying when someone unfamiliar picks them up. Separation anxiety, protest when the caregiver leaves, often peaks between about 10 and 18 months. Both are signs that attachment is working: the baby knows who her people are. Toddlers use the attached adult as a base, wandering off to explore and running back to check in. A toddler who never checks in, or who is equally happy with any adult, is a child to watch.

Every child also arrives with a *temperament*, an inborn style of reacting. Some babies are easy to soothe, settle into routines and greet new things with interest. Some are slow to warm up, hanging back before joining. Some are intense, with big reactions to noise, hunger, change and joy. None of these is a flaw, and a temperament is not a personality problem to fix. The adult's job is to fit the care to the child: extra warning before a change for the slow-to-warm child, a calm room for the intense one.

Emotional skills grow in a rough order. Toddlers feel everything at full strength and cannot yet manage it, which is what a tantrum is: a feeling bigger than the child's tools. Preschoolers learn to name feelings, mad, sad, scared, and to use words instead of teeth. School-age children learn to wait, to lose a game without falling apart, to keep a friend through a disagreement. The adult teaches all of this mostly by example: naming feelings out loud, staying calm, and coming back after a hard moment.

words.d: the deep, lasting bond between a child and the caregiver who reliably responds to the child's needs
learning to relate to other people: trust, play, sharing, friendship
learning to feel, recognize, name and manage emotions
a child's inborn style of reacting: easy, slow to warm up or intense; not a flaw and not a choice

look.title: First Day at the Toddler Room
look.text: Three 18-month-olds start at a child care center on the same Monday. Jonah walks in, drops his father's hand and heads for the blocks. Priya clings to her mother's leg, cries when she leaves, and after ten minutes is watching the other children from the reading corner. Marcus screams for twenty minutes, throws a toy, and then falls asleep in the teacher's lap. By Friday all three are playing.
look.prompt: Match each child to a temperament type. Which one would you have been most tempted to label as a problem, and why would that label be wrong?

check.q: A nine-month-old who used to go happily to anyone now cries when a visiting aunt picks him up. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: The aunt did something to frighten him
He is becoming spoiled by too much holding
Stranger anxiety, a normal sign that attachment to his own caregivers is working
He has a hearing problem and did not recognize her voice
check.why: Stranger anxiety commonly appears at about 6 to 9 months. It shows the baby now knows who his people are, which is a healthy attachment milestone.

check.q: Which caregiver behavior does the most to build secure attachment in an infant?
choices: Letting the baby cry for long stretches so she learns to self-soothe
Keeping the baby with a different adult each day so she adapts
Buying developmental toys for every stage
Responding reliably and warmly when the baby cries or reaches out
check.why: Attachment is built by repeated experience that a need brings a response. Reliable, warm responding is the core of it.

check.q: A two-year-old screams and drops to the floor when told it is time to leave the park. Which description fits best?
choices: A tantrum: a feeling bigger than the tools a toddler has to manage it
Manipulation that must be punished so it stops
A sign of a difficult temperament that needs correction
Egocentrism that will be outgrown by age 3
check.why: Toddlers feel at full strength and have almost no tools yet for managing feelings. A tantrum is that gap, not a plan.

sections.title: Stages From Birth to School Age

lessons.title: The First Year
lessons.mainIdea: In the first year a baby goes from reflexes to walking and from crying to first words, and a caregiver's job is to respond, protect and talk.
reading: A newborn arrives with reflexes and not much else. Touch her cheek and she turns toward it, rooting for milk. Put a finger in her palm and she grips. Startle her and her arms fly out. She sleeps 14 to 17 hours a day in short stretches and eats every 2 to 3 hours. She can see about 8 to 12 inches, roughly the distance to the face of whoever is feeding her, and she prefers faces to anything else. *Infancy*, the first year of life, begins here and ends with a child who walks, points, and says a word or two.

By about 2 months many babies smile at a face and coo. At about 4 to 6 months they babble, rolling out strings like "ba-ba-ba," laugh, roll over, and reach for things. Around 6 months many can sit with support and are ready to start solid foods alongside milk. At about 6 to 9 months they sit alone, pass a toy from hand to hand, and show stranger anxiety. Between about 9 and 12 months many crawl, pull to stand, cruise along furniture, use the pincer grasp, wave, point, respond to their name and say a first word, often "mama," "dada" or "ball."

The caregiver's work in this year is three things. Respond: pick the baby up, feed her when hungry, change her when wet, and do not worry about spoiling; an infant cannot be spoiled by being answered. Protect: put her on her back to sleep, on a firm flat surface with nothing else in the crib, never shake her, and keep her out of the *danger zone* of hot liquids, small objects and unfenced stairs. Talk: narrate what you are doing, name what she looks at, read to her from the first months. The number of words a baby hears in the first year shapes the number of words she will say.

What to bring to the doctor in the first year: a baby who does not respond to loud sounds, does not smile at people by about 3 months, does not reach for things by about 6 months, cannot sit with help by about 9 months, or does not babble, point or respond to her name by about 12 months. Any single one may mean nothing. Checkups exist so a professional can look.

words.d: the first year of life, from birth to about 12 months
an automatic movement a newborn makes without deciding to, such as rooting, gripping or startling
the repeated consonant-vowel sounds, like ba-ba-ba, that many babies begin at about 4 to 6 months
in child care, anything within a baby's reach that can burn, choke or cause a fall; in the kitchen, 40 to 140 °F

look.title: Two Hours With a Six-Month-Old
look.text: You are watching your neighbor's six-month-old for two hours on a Saturday afternoon. She has just been fed. In the living room there is a play mat, a basket of board books, a bowl of grapes on the coffee table, a phone charger plugged in at floor level, and a soft blanket in the crib where she naps. The neighbor says, "She usually naps around three. Just put her down on her tummy, she likes it."
look.prompt: List every change you would make to the room and to the nap plan before the neighbor leaves, and give the rule behind each one.

check.q: A parent worries that picking up their three-month-old every time he cries will spoil him. What is the right response?
choices: Wait five minutes each time so he learns patience
An infant cannot be spoiled by being answered; responding builds trust
Let him cry it out at night but respond during the day
Pick him up only if he is hungry or wet
check.why: In the first year, reliable responding is how attachment and trust form. Spoiling is not a risk with an infant.

check.q: Which first-year sign would be a reason to talk to the doctor?
choices: Not crawling at 9 months but scooting on the bottom
Not walking alone at 12 months
A 12-month-old who does not babble, point or respond to her name
Crying when a stranger picks her up at 8 months
check.why: Babbling, pointing and responding to a name are expected by about 12 months. Skipping crawling, walking at 13 months and stranger anxiety are all within normal range.

check.q: How should a caregiver put a four-month-old down for a nap?
choices: On her stomach so she sleeps longer
On her side with a rolled towel to keep her there
On her back in a crib with a soft blanket and a bumper pad
On her back on a firm flat surface with nothing else in the crib
check.why: Safe sleep is on the back, on a firm flat surface, with no blankets, pillows, bumpers or toys in the sleep space.

lessons.title: Toddlers, One to Three
lessons.mainIdea: Toddlers are driven to do it themselves, and the caregiver's job is to make the home safe enough to let them, and to set a few firm, calm limits.
reading: A 20-month-old wants to put on her own shoes. It takes six minutes and the shoes end up on the wrong feet. Her father wants to do it in ten seconds. This small standoff is the whole of toddlerhood. A *toddler*, about 1 to 3 years old, is discovering that she is a separate person with her own will, and she wants to use it. "No" and "me do it" are not defiance. They are the sound of a self forming. The adult who understands that saves himself two years of arguments.

The body: many toddlers walk well by about 15 months, run by about 2, climb stairs holding a hand, kick a ball, and by 3 pedal a tricycle and jump with both feet. Fine motor: scribbling, stacking a few blocks, turning pages, using a spoon with spills, and by about 3 drawing a circle and dressing with help. The mind: pretend play begins, simple puzzles, sorting shapes, following two-step directions. Toilet training readiness usually appears somewhere between about 18 months and 3 years, and pushing it before the child shows signs of readiness usually makes it take longer.

The words: many toddlers say about 50 words by 2 and put two words together, "more juice," "daddy go." By 3 many speak in short sentences that a stranger can mostly understand. The feelings: this is the age of the tantrum. Toddlers want two things at once, cannot wait, cannot explain, and have no brakes. The caregiver provides the brakes from outside: a calm voice, a short clear limit, a choice between two acceptable things, and a body that stays close while the storm passes.

The rule for toddlers is *autonomy* within safety. Childproof the space so that most of what she can reach is allowed, and "no" is saved for the few things that matter. Offer real choices: the red cup or the blue cup, not "do you want to get dressed?" Give warnings before a change: "two more slides and then we go." Expect messes, expect repetition, and expect to hear the same book read forty times. That is not stubbornness; it is how a toddler learns.

words.d: a child about 1 to 3 years old, from walking to about the age of short sentences
a child's drive to act as a separate person and do things for herself; the central task of toddlerhood
a toddler's full-strength outburst when a feeling is bigger than the child's ability to manage it

look.title: Shoes, Six Minutes
look.text: It is 7:40 a.m. and the family must leave at 7:45. A 20-month-old sits on the floor working her left shoe onto her right foot. Her father says, "Let me," and reaches for the shoe. She screams "Me do it!" and throws the shoe. He picks her up, puts both shoes on while she kicks, and carries her to the car crying. He is late anyway.
look.prompt: Rewrite the morning. Change one thing before 7:40 and one thing the father says at 7:40 so that the shoes go on and nobody screams. Name the toddler principle behind each change.

check.q: Which is the best way to offer a toddler a choice?
choices: "The red cup or the blue cup?"
"Do you want to drink your milk?"
"Which cup, and which chair, and which spoon, and do you want a straw?"
"You will use the red cup because I said so."
check.why: A toddler choice is between two acceptable options. A yes-or-no question invites "no," and too many choices overwhelm.

check.q: A two-year-old says about 50 words and puts two together, like "more milk." How does this compare with the common range?
choices: Far behind; most two-year-olds speak in full sentences
Typical for about age 2
Far ahead; most two-year-olds have only a few words
Impossible to say without a hearing test
check.why: About 50 words and two-word phrases by age 2 is the commonly cited milestone. Short sentences usually come by about 3.

check.q: Why does childproofing a home make a toddler easier to guide, not just safer?
choices: Because a childproofed home needs no supervision
Because toddlers stop exploring once cabinets are locked
Because "no" is saved for the few things that matter, so it keeps its meaning
Because childproofing teaches the toddler which things are dangerous
check.why: When most of what a toddler can reach is allowed, the adult says "no" rarely, and the toddler learns it means something.

lessons.title: Preschool, Three to Five
lessons.mainIdea: Preschoolers learn through play and questions, and they need adults who answer honestly, set up turns and let them do real jobs.
reading: Ask a four-year-old why the sky is blue and be ready for the next question, and the one after that. The *preschool* years, about 3 to 5, are the age of "why." A preschooler can now hold ideas in his head, talk about things that are not in front of him, and play a game with rules that last more than a minute. He is also still egocentric, still thinks in pictures more than logic, and still cannot always tell what he wished from what happened. When he says the dog broke the lamp, he may half believe it.

The body: by 4 many preschoolers hop on one foot, catch a bounced ball, climb a playground ladder, and by 5 skip and swing themselves. Fine motor: cutting with child scissors along a line, holding a crayon with fingers instead of a fist, copying a square, drawing a person with a head and a few parts, and by 5 writing some letters. The mind: counting to 10 or beyond, naming colors, sorting by size, following three-step directions, understanding "same" and "different," and retelling a story in order. Speech is mostly clear by 4 and fully understandable by 5.

Socially this is the age when play changes shape. Two-year-olds play beside each other. Three-year-olds begin to play with each other, and by 4 or 5 many can plan a game together, assign parts and argue about the rules, which is a skill in itself. Sharing does not come naturally; it is taught by setting up turns and using a timer. Friendships form and break by the hour. Fears appear, of the dark, of dogs, of the drain in the bathtub, and they are real to the child even when they are not real to the adult.

The caregiver's tools: answer questions honestly and briefly, then let the child ask the next one. Give real jobs, setting the table, feeding the cat, sorting laundry by color, because a preschooler who is trusted with a task learns *initiative*, the willingness to start things. Read every day. Limit screens and choose slow ones. Set a few clear rules and keep them the same every time. When he lies about the lamp, skip the trial: "The lamp is broken. Let's clean it up together, and next time tell me right away."

words.d: about age 3 to 5, from short sentences to the start of kindergarten
the willingness to start a task on one's own; preschoolers build it when adults trust them with real jobs
play in which children plan together, take parts and follow shared rules, common by about 4 or 5

look.title: The Broken Lamp
look.text: You come into the living room and the lamp is on the floor, cracked. The four-year-old is standing next to it with a ball in his hand. "The dog did it," he says. The dog is asleep in the kitchen. His older sister, who is nine, says, "He's lying, punish him."
look.prompt: Write what you say to the four-year-old, in three sentences or fewer, and explain why a long lecture about lying would not work at this age.

check.q: Two four-year-olds both want the only red truck. Which adult response best teaches sharing?
choices: Take the truck away so nobody gets it
Tell them sharing is nice and walk away
Give it to the one who asked first, permanently
Set up turns with a timer: three minutes each, then switch
check.why: Sharing is taught, not assumed. A concrete turn with a visible timer gives preschoolers a structure they can follow.

check.q: Which preschool milestone is commonly expected by about age 4?
choices: Hopping on one foot
Reading a simple book alone
Riding a two-wheel bike without training wheels
Writing a full sentence
check.why: Hopping on one foot is a common 4-year-old gross motor milestone. Reading, sentences and two-wheel bikes come later for most children.

check.q: A four-year-old is terrified of the bathtub drain. What is the best approach?
choices: Tell her it is silly and put her in the tub anyway
Treat the fear as real to her, drain the tub after she is out, and let her watch from a distance
Skip baths until she outgrows it
Explain in detail how the plumbing works so she reasons her way out of the fear
check.why: Preschool fears are real to the child and are outgrown with patience, not argument. Reducing the trigger and staying calm works better than logic at this age.

lessons.title: School Age, Six to Twelve
lessons.mainIdea: School-age children build competence and friendships, and they need adults who notice effort, keep rules fair and stay available as the peer world grows.
reading: A nine-year-old comes home, drops her backpack and announces that she is never going back to school because Jasmine sat with someone else at lunch. Twenty minutes later she is on the phone with Jasmine, laughing. Welcome to the *school-age* years, about 6 to 12. The child now lives in two worlds: the family and the peer group, and the second one grows every year. She is also becoming capable in a way that surprises adults: she can read for information, keep a promise, follow a recipe, remember a schedule and argue a point with logic.

The body grows steadily, about 2 to 3 inches a year, with the growth spurt of puberty beginning for some children toward the end of this stage, often earlier for girls than for boys. Coordination improves: real sports, bike riding, handwriting that others can read, cooking with supervision, sewing a running stitch. The mind takes the big step the preschooler could not: logical thinking about concrete things. A seven-year-old knows the juice is the same amount in the tall glass. A ten-year-old can plan a project in steps, understand another person's point of view, and tell a fair rule from an unfair one, loudly.

Socially, friendships deepen and become more about loyalty and shared interests. Belonging matters intensely, and so does being good at something. The main task of these years is *competence*: the feeling of being able to do real things well. Children who find something they are good at, a sport, an instrument, drawing, reading, cooking, carry that confidence into the harder years ahead. Children who mostly hear what they cannot do learn to expect failure. The adult's job is to notice effort and specific progress, not just results.

What to watch: a child who has no friends at all over a long stretch, who suddenly refuses school, whose sleep or eating changes sharply, who stops doing things she loved, or who has bruises or fears she cannot explain. Any of these is a reason to ask gently and, if the answer worries you, to bring in a counselor, a doctor or, when abuse is possible, the people whose job it is to protect children. Most of the time, the nine-year-old is back on the phone in twenty minutes. Being available is the skill.

words.d: about age 6 to 12, from the start of school to the beginning of adolescence
the feeling of being able to do real things well; the central task of the school-age years
children of about the same age whose opinions and friendship matter more each year of school age

look.title: The Science Fair Volcano
look.text: A ten-year-old builds a science fair volcano. It is lopsided, the paint is streaky, and the eruption is weak. His father says, "It's fine, but Alex's had a working pump. Next year I'll help you build something better." The boy takes the volcano to his room and does not enter the fair the next year.
look.prompt: The father meant to be encouraging. Rewrite his sentence so it builds competence instead of comparing, and name the two things he could have noticed specifically.

check.q: Which comment best builds competence in a school-age child who just cooked scrambled eggs with some shell in them?
choices: "Next time let me do it."
"Your sister never gets shell in hers."
"You cracked all four eggs yourself and kept the heat low so they didn't burn. Next time try cracking on a flat surface."
"Good job!"
check.why: Competence grows from specific noticing of effort and progress plus one concrete next step. Comparison and vague praise do less.

check.q: A seven-year-old now understands that the amount of juice does not change when poured into a taller glass. What has developed?
choices: Object permanence
Fine motor control
Egocentrism
Logical thinking about concrete things
check.why: Understanding that amount stays the same across a change of shape marks the shift to concrete logical thinking, usually at about 6 or 7.

check.q: Which school-age change is a reason to ask questions and possibly get help, rather than wait it out?
choices: A sudden refusal to go to school that lasts for weeks, with changes in sleep and eating
A best friend who changes every month
Announcing she will never go back to school after a lunch-table fight
Wanting to spend more time with friends than with family
check.why: A lasting school refusal with sleep and eating changes is a warning pattern. Shifting friendships and dramatic announcements are typical of the age.

lessons.title: Play Is the Work
lessons.mainIdea: Play is how children practice every domain at once, and the best play materials are open-ended, safe for the age and matched to the stage.
reading: Watch a three-year-old with a cardboard box for twenty minutes. It is a car, then a house, then a boat, then a hat. She climbs in and out (gross motor), folds the flaps (fine motor), decides it is a boat and needs a paddle (symbolic thinking), invites her brother aboard and assigns him the job of shark (social), and cries when the box tears and then recovers (emotional). Nobody taught her any of this. *Play* is the way children practice every domain at once, and it is not a break from learning. It is the learning.

Play changes shape with the stage. Infants play with their senses and with you: peek-a-boo, rattles, mirrors, being bounced. Toddlers do *parallel play*, sitting beside another child, each doing their own thing, occasionally grabbing. Around 3 children start playing together, and by 4 or 5 they plan games with parts and rules. School-age children add organized games, collections, building projects and long pretend stories that continue for days. Rough-and-tumble play, chasing and wrestling, is normal and useful as long as everyone is still laughing.

The best toys are the ones that do the least. A toy that sings and lights up when a button is pressed does one thing. Blocks, play dough, dress-up clothes, a doll, crayons and paper, a set of plastic cups, a pile of leaves, a cardboard box: these are *open-ended*, they can be a hundred things, and the child supplies the ideas. Match materials to the age. Under 3, nothing that fits through a toilet-paper tube, because it can be swallowed or choked on. Preschoolers can handle small pieces with supervision. Check every toy for loose parts, sharp edges and long cords.

The adult's role in play is mostly to set the stage and get out of the way. Give time, at least an hour of unstructured play a day for a preschooler, and space, and materials, and then let the child lead. When you do join, follow: if she says the block is a phone, it is a phone. Ask open questions, "what happens next?" rather than quizzing, "what color is that?" And do not fix the lopsided tower. The falling is the point.

words.d: self-chosen, enjoyable activity through which children practice physical, cognitive, social and emotional skills
toddlers playing beside each other without playing together; normal at about 1 to 3
a material that can be used many ways, such as blocks or play dough, so the child supplies the ideas

look.title: Choosing for the Toddler Room
look.text: A child care center has $200 (example) to spend on the room for children aged 1 to 3. On the list: a set of large wooden blocks ($60), a talking alphabet tablet with a screen ($45), a bin of plastic cups and bowls ($15), a 100-piece bead-stringing kit ($20), two child-size brooms and a dustpan ($25), a plush ride-on horse that plays songs ($55), and a roll of butcher paper with fat crayons ($20).
look.prompt: Pick the items you would buy within the $200 and name one item you would refuse even if it were free, with the rule that makes it unsafe for this age.

check.q: Two 18-month-olds sit on the same rug, each stacking their own cups, not looking at each other. What kind of play is this?
choices: Cooperative play
Parallel play, which is typical for toddlers
A sign that they are not socially developing
Rough-and-tumble play
check.why: Playing beside another child without playing with them is parallel play, the normal pattern at about 1 to 3.

check.q: Which toy is the most open-ended?
choices: A doll that says six phrases when squeezed
A puzzle with one right solution
A set of plain wooden blocks
A video game with a set story
check.why: Blocks can be anything the child decides. The other three each do one fixed thing, so the child supplies less of the idea.

check.q: A preschooler says her block is a telephone and hands it to you. What is the best response?
choices: "That's a block, not a phone. Can you say block?"
"Let's build a tower with it instead."
"Blocks go in the bin when we're done."
Hold it to your ear and say, "Hello? Who's calling?"
check.why: In play the adult follows the child's lead. Accepting the pretend supports symbolic thinking and language.

lessons.title: How Language Grows
lessons.mainIdea: Language grows from being talked to, and its milestones, from cooing to sentences, are the ones most worth watching because they are easiest to help early.
reading: A father changes a diaper and narrates the whole thing. "Now the wipe, it's cold, isn't it? Now the clean diaper. Now the snaps, one, two, three." The baby is four months old and understands none of it. She is also learning all of it. *Language development* runs on input: the number and variety of words a child hears, spoken directly to her, in a warm voice, about what is happening right now. Television and background talk do not count nearly as much. A face, a voice and a thing to look at together is how the wiring gets built.

The milestones, as ranges: cooing at about 2 months; babbling at about 4 to 6 months; responding to her own name at about 6 to 9 months; first words at about 10 to 14 months; about 50 words and two-word phrases by about 2; short sentences and about 200 to 300 words by about 3; mostly clear speech that a stranger understands by about 4. Understanding runs ahead of speaking the whole way. A one-year-old who says three words may understand fifty. A child growing up with two languages may say fewer words in each at first, and that is not a delay; count the words in both languages together.

What helps: talk about what the child is looking at, not what you want her to look at. Expand what she says: she says "dog," you say "yes, a big brown dog." Read every day and let her turn the pages, point, and hear the same book many times. Sing. Wait: after you ask something, count to five in your head before filling the silence. What does not help: correcting pronunciation ("say it right"), quizzing, or talking baby talk instead of real words. "Baba" is fine from the baby; "bottle" is what she needs to hear from you.

Language is the domain where early help matters most, because the years before 5 are when the brain is most ready for it. A child who does not babble by about 9 months, has no words by about 16 months, has no two-word phrases by about 2, or loses words she once had, should have her hearing checked and be seen by a doctor. Hearing is the first thing to test; a child who has had many ear infections may simply not be hearing clearly. Speech therapy, started early, is short and effective. Waiting to see is the one thing not to do.

words.d: the growth of understanding and using words, from cooing to sentences
repeating a child's words back with more added: the child says "dog," the adult says "a big brown dog"
the words a child understands, which always run ahead of the words the child can say

look.title: Rough Spoken Vocabulary by Age
look.cite: Approximate figures commonly cited in child development guides; ranges are wide and understanding runs well ahead of speech
look.prompt: Between which two ages does spoken vocabulary grow the fastest, and what does that tell a caregiver about how much to talk during those months?

check.q: A toddler points and says "truck." Which adult reply does the most for language growth?
choices: "Yes, a big red truck! It's going fast."
"Say it again, louder."
"Truck. Good. What color is it? What's this? And this?"
"Uh-huh."
check.why: Expanding the child's word with more language about the same thing is the most effective everyday technique. Quizzing and one-word replies add little.

check.q: A 16-month-old raised in a Spanish-speaking and English-speaking home says four words in Spanish and three in English. How should this be judged?
choices: As a delay, because seven words is too few for either language
By counting all seven words together, which is within the usual range
As a sign one language should be dropped
By counting only the words in the language of the school
check.why: For a child learning two languages, count words in both together. Seven words at 16 months is within the common range.

check.q: Which sign is a clear reason to have a child's hearing checked and see a doctor?
choices: A two-year-old who says "wawa" for water
A three-year-old whose grandmother cannot understand every word
A two-year-old with no two-word phrases who has stopped using words she had
A one-year-old who understands "no" but says only two words
check.why: Losing words once gained, and no two-word phrases by about 2, are warning signs. The other three are within normal range.

lessons.title: Every Child, Their Own Path
lessons.mainIdea: Every child develops differently, including children with disabilities; the caregiver's job is to know the ranges, watch for the real warning signs and get help early without shame.
reading: In a kindergarten class of twenty, one child reads chapter books and one is still learning letters. One runs faster than anyone and cannot sit through a story. One speaks three languages and one has a stutter. One uses a wheelchair, one wears hearing aids, one has an IEP for autism and needs the schedule on the wall to get through the day. Every one of them is developing. The ranges in this chapter describe what many children do. They do not describe what every child must do, and a child who is outside a range is not a lesser child. He is a child whose path is different and who may need different support.

A *developmental delay* means a child is reaching milestones noticeably later than the usual range in one or more domains. Sometimes it resolves on its own. Sometimes it is the first sign of a *disability*, a lasting condition that affects how a child moves, learns, communicates or relates. Cerebral palsy affects movement. Down syndrome affects learning and often speech. Autism affects communication and social interaction, often with strong interests and sensitivity to sound and touch. Hearing and vision loss affect everything downstream of them. None of these is caused by anything a parent did, and none of them is a reason to expect less love, less play or less joy.

What to do when something seems off: first, write down what you see, with dates. "Does not respond to name, 14 months, three tries today." Second, tell the doctor, plainly and early; do not wait for the next scheduled checkup if the concern is real. Third, know that help exists and is free to ask for. In the United States, children under 3 with delays can be evaluated through their state's early intervention program at no cost to the family, and children 3 and older through the public schools. The earlier support starts, the more it helps. Waiting to see is the most common mistake and the most costly one.

The principle for anyone who cares for children: know the ranges so you can relax about what is normal, watch the order and the direction, and when a child loses a skill, stops gaining skills or is well past the late end of a range, speak up, kindly and without blame. Then keep doing what you did before: talk, play, read, respond and enjoy the child who is actually in front of you. Mateo's pediatrician did not say "he is fine." She said "he is on time, and here is what I am watching." That is the whole skill.

words.d: reaching milestones noticeably later than the usual range in one or more domains; may resolve or may signal a lasting condition
a lasting condition that affects how a child moves, learns, communicates or relates to others
free evaluation and support services for children under 3 with delays, provided through each state; schools serve children 3 and older
Individualized Education Program: a written plan of school supports and goals for a student with a disability

look.title: Three Notes in a Babysitter's Notebook
look.text: Note 1: "Lily, 15 months, not walking, crawls and cruises, waved bye-bye." Note 2: "Sam, 2 years 2 months, no words, used to say 'ball' and 'mama' at 15 months, doesn't turn when I call him from behind." Note 3: "Noor, 4, only wants to line up cars, covers ears at the blender, talks about planets for twenty minutes, doesn't look at me when I talk."
look.prompt: For each note, decide: within range, worth mentioning to the parent, or urgent to mention to the parent and doctor. Give the specific sign that decided it.

check.q: A babysitter notices a 2-year-old has stopped saying the few words he used to say and does not turn when called from behind. What is the best action?
choices: Wait until he is 3, since boys often talk late
Try flashcards every visit to build his vocabulary
Assume it is because he is learning two languages
Tell the parents specifically what she saw, with dates, and suggest a hearing check and a doctor visit
check.why: Losing words and not responding to sound are warning signs in any child. Hearing is checked first, and early help is the most effective.

check.q: Which statement about children with disabilities is accurate?
choices: A child with a disability is still developing and benefits from the same talk, play and responsiveness as every child
A disability means development has stopped
Most disabilities are caused by something the parent did in the first year
Children with disabilities should not be compared with milestone ranges at all, so no one should watch their progress
check.why: Development continues on a different path. Talk, play, reading and responsive care help every child, and progress is still watched and supported.

check.q: A family suspects their 2-year-old has a delay but is worried about the cost of an evaluation. What should they know?
choices: Evaluations are only available through private specialists
Their state's early intervention program evaluates children under 3 at no cost to the family
They must wait until kindergarten for the school to evaluate
Insurance is the only way to pay for it
check.why: Every state's early intervention program evaluates children under 3 for free. Public schools take over at age 3.

review.q: Which sequence lists gross motor milestones in the usual order?
choices: Walk, sit, roll over, hold head steady
Sit, hold head steady, walk, roll over
Hold head steady, roll over, sit, walk
Roll over, walk, sit, hold head steady
review.why: Physical control develops head to toe: head, then trunk (rolling, sitting), then legs (standing, walking).

review.q: A baby pulls a blanket off a hidden toy for the first time. Which domain and milestone is this?
choices: Physical: pincer grasp
Social: stranger anxiety
Emotional: attachment
Cognitive: object permanence
review.why: Searching for a hidden object shows the baby knows it still exists, which is object permanence, a cognitive milestone at about 6 to 10 months.

review.q: A grandmother says her 11-month-old grandson is "behind" because his cousin walked at 10 months. What is the most accurate reply?
choices: Walking alone commonly happens anywhere from about 9 to 15 months, so 11 months and not walking is on time
He should see a specialist right away
Boys always walk later than girls, so it is fine
He should be put in a walker every day to catch up
review.why: Milestones are ranges. Eleven months is inside the usual walking range, and comparing cousins tells you nothing about a problem.

review.q: Which caregiver action most directly builds an infant's trust?
choices: Buying a crib mobile with music
Responding reliably and warmly when the baby cries
Feeding on a strict schedule regardless of hunger
Rotating caregivers daily so the baby adapts
review.why: Attachment forms through repeated experience that a need brings a response. Reliable, warm responding is what builds it.

review.q: A three-year-old plays beside another child on the same rug, each with her own dolls, without playing together. This is:
choices: Cooperative play
A sign of a social delay
Parallel play, normal at this age
Rough-and-tumble play
review.why: Parallel play is the common pattern from about 1 to 3, and children begin playing together at about 3 to 4.

review.q: Which of these is a warning sign that should send a family to the doctor rather than a normal variation?
choices: A 9-month-old who scoots instead of crawling
A 2-year-old who says "pasghetti"
A 4-year-old who is afraid of the dark
A 2-year-old who has lost words she used to say
review.why: Losing a skill once gained is a warning sign in any domain. Scooting, mispronunciations and preschool fears are all within normal range.

review.q: A toddler is told, "Do you want to put your coat on?" and says "No!" What would have worked better?
choices: A choice between two acceptable options, such as "the blue coat or the red one?"
A longer explanation of why coats matter in winter
Asking again in a firmer voice
Offering a candy for putting the coat on
review.why: Toddlers are building autonomy. A yes-or-no question invites "no"; a choice between two acceptable things gives the child a real say inside a limit.

review.q: A four-year-old, told to share a toy, refuses. Which understanding of the stage leads to the best response?
choices: Sharing is natural by 4, so refusal means the child is selfish
Sharing is taught; setting up concrete turns with a timer works better than telling
Four-year-olds cannot share at all, so remove the toy
Only school-age children can be expected to take turns
review.why: Preschoolers are still egocentric and learn sharing through structure. A visible turn with a timer is the tool.

chapters.title: Guidance and Safe Care
chapters.bigQuestion: What does it take to keep a child safe and guide their behavior for an evening, a week or a childhood?

story.title: The List on the Fridge
story.kicker: Dani's first paid babysitting job started with a sheet of paper under a magnet, and by nine o'clock she had used every line of it.
paragraphs: Dani was sixteen and had been asked to watch the Okafor kids, Zuri, who was four, and baby Kofi, who was seven months, from six to ten on a Friday. She had her Red Cross babysitting card and a bag with a coloring book, a deck of cards and her phone charger. Mrs. Okafor met her at the door already holding her keys, and walked her straight to the refrigerator.

Under a magnet was a single sheet. Their cell numbers. The pediatrician's number. Poison Control, 1-800-222-1222, written in red. The address of the house, because, Mrs. Okafor said, "if you ever have to call 911 you will not remember it." Zuri: allergic to peanuts, EpiPen in the top kitchen drawer, here is how it works, watch me. Kofi: bottle at seven, six ounces, then bed at seven-thirty, on his back, in the crib, nothing in it, sleep sack only. Zuri: bath optional, teeth, two books, lights out at eight, she will ask for a third book, the answer is no. Dani read it twice.

The evening went the way evenings with a four-year-old go. Zuri did not want the chicken; Dani gave her the choice of eating it with ketchup or with the rice mixed in, and she ate it with ketchup. Zuri wanted to climb the bookshelf; Dani did not say "no" thirty times, she got out the couch cushions and made a fort, and the bookshelf was forgotten. Kofi took his bottle, went into his sleep sack, and Dani laid him on his back and stood there a moment, checking the crib the way the card had taught her: firm mattress, fitted sheet, nothing else.

At eight-forty, with Zuri asleep, Dani heard a small sound and found Kofi awake and coughing, red-faced, and for one long second she could not tell whether he was choking or just crying. Then he drew a full breath and howled, and she picked him up and walked him and he settled. Her hands shook. She had known exactly what to do for an infant who could not breathe, five back blows, five chest thrusts, call 911, and she had been ready to do it. She was very glad she had not needed to.

When the Okafors came home Dani told them everything, including the cough, in order, the way the list had been written. Mrs. Okafor said the thing that made Dani a regular for two years: "You didn't just follow the list. You knew why every line was there." This chapter is that list, and the reasons.
story.think: Every line on the refrigerator list was there for a reason. Pick two lines and explain what could go wrong on an ordinary Friday night if that line were missing.

lessons.title: Guidance, Not Punishment
lessons.mainIdea: Guidance teaches a child what to do; punishment only teaches what to avoid when an adult is watching, and hitting a child teaches that hitting works.
reading: A three-year-old throws a cup of milk on the floor. One adult yells, grabs her arm and puts her in a chair facing the wall for ten minutes. Another adult says, "Milk stays in the cup. Here's a towel; let's wipe it up," and hands her the towel. Both adults want the same thing: no more milk on the floor. Only the second one is teaching it. *Guidance* is everything an adult does to help a child learn how to behave. *Punishment* is making a child suffer for what she already did. The first builds a skill. The second builds fear, and fear stops working the moment the adult leaves the room.

The case against spanking is not about being soft. Decades of research have found that children who are hit are more aggressive, not less, and are no better behaved over time. Hitting teaches, very clearly, that a bigger person may hit a smaller one when angry. It also damages the trust that makes every other kind of guidance possible. Yelling and shaming do a milder version of the same harm. And shaking a baby, ever, for any reason, can cause permanent brain injury or death. A crying baby who cannot be soothed goes in the crib on his back, safe, while the adult steps out to breathe.

Guidance starts with expectations that match the age. A one-year-old cannot remember a rule from yesterday. A two-year-old cannot share. A three-year-old cannot sit still for a forty-minute dinner. A four-year-old cannot always tell wishes from facts. Most "misbehavior" in young children is a child doing exactly what a child that age does, in a situation that was set up for an adult. Half of guidance is changing the setup: the fragile thing goes on a high shelf, dinner is twenty minutes, the walk to the car starts with a two-minute warning.

The other half is a small set of tools, taught in the next two lessons: routines, choices, redirection, and natural and logical consequences. Behind all of them is one attitude. The adult is calm, the adult is kind, and the adult means it. A limit stated once in a quiet voice and kept every time is worth more than a threat shouted ten times. Children test limits to find out if they are real. The answer should be boring: yes, every time.

words.d: everything an adult does to help a child learn how to behave, from setting up the room to stating limits calmly
making a child suffer for a past action; it builds fear and avoidance rather than skill
a clear rule about what is allowed, stated calmly and kept the same every time
permanent brain injury or death caused by shaking an infant; never shake a baby for any reason

lessons.title: Routines and Choices
lessons.mainIdea: A predictable routine prevents most battles, and a choice between two acceptable options gives a child real power inside the adult's limit.
reading: Bedtime at the Okafor house goes: bath, pajamas, teeth, two books, song, lights out. Every night. In that order. By the time Zuri was three she could recite it, and mostly she did not fight it, because there was nothing to fight. It was simply what happened after dinner. This is a *routine*: a fixed order of events that happens the same way every time. Routines work because young children cannot tell time and cannot plan, so an unpredictable day feels like a series of ambushes. A predictable day lets the child know what is coming and get ready for it.

Build routines around the hard parts of the day: waking up, leaving the house, meals, naps, cleanup and bedtime. Keep the order the same even when the times shift. Use *transitions*, warnings that a change is coming: "two more turns on the slide, then shoes." Toddlers and preschoolers hate being interrupted mid-thought as much as adults do; a warning lets them finish. A picture chart of the bedtime steps on the wall lets a preschooler run the routine herself, which she will proudly do. School-age children can help write the routine, and children who help write a rule follow it far more often.

Inside a routine, give *choices*. The rule is two options, both of which the adult can live with. "Red cup or blue cup?" "Walk to the car or hop to the car?" "Bath before books or after?" What the choice does is hand the child a small piece of real power at the exact moment she was about to grab for it by saying no. What it must not be is fake. "Do you want to go to bed now?" is not a choice, because the honest answer is no and the adult will not accept it. And "Which do you want, the couch, the chair, the floor, the rug, or my lap?" is too many; a three-year-old freezes.

The principle: most conflict with young children is about control, and a routine plus a choice gives the child control over the things that do not matter so the adult can keep control over the things that do. When Zuri asks for a third book, the answer is no, calmly, the same way every night. Because everything else about bedtime is hers, the no is easy to take.

words.d: a fixed order of daily events that happens the same way every time, so the child knows what is coming
the change from one activity to the next; a warning before it prevents most protests
in guidance, two acceptable options offered to the child so the child has real power inside the adult's limit

check.q: Which of these is a real choice for a three-year-old?

"Do you want to go to bed or stay up?"
"Pick any pajamas from the whole drawer."

check.why: A real choice offers two options the adult can accept. A yes-or-no question invites no, and an open drawer is too many choices.

check.q: A preschooler screams every time she is told playtime is over. What is the most useful change?
choices: Give a warning a few minutes before the change: "two more turns, then cleanup"
End playtime earlier so she has less to lose
Stop announcing the end and just take the toys away
Let her play until she chooses to stop
check.why: Transition warnings let a child finish a thought and get ready. Most protests at a change are about being interrupted without notice.

check.q: Why does a fixed bedtime routine reduce arguments?
choices: Because it makes the child too tired to argue
Because young children cannot plan or tell time, so a predictable order removes the surprise that causes the protest
Because it lets the adult skip the steps the child dislikes

check.why: A young child cannot see the day ahead. A routine tells her what comes next, so a change stops feeling like an ambush.

lessons.title: Redirection and Consequences
lessons.mainIdea: Redirect a young child toward what is allowed, and let older children learn from consequences that follow naturally or logically from what they did.
reading: A fourteen-month-old is pulling books off the shelf and chewing on the covers. Saying "no" gets a look and then more chewing, because to a fourteen-month-old "no" is a sound, not a plan. *Redirection* is the tool: take the book gently, hand him a teething ring or a board book that is his to chew, and move him three feet away. "Books are for reading. This one is for chewing." Redirection works for infants and toddlers because it replaces the forbidden thing with an allowed one instead of leaving a hole where the fun was. It works best when the replacement is close by and at least as interesting.

For preschoolers and older, add *natural consequences*: what happens by itself when a child makes a choice, with no adult adding anything. She refuses her coat; she is cold on the walk. He leaves his truck in the driveway; it gets run over. She does not eat dinner; she is hungry before bed and gets the same dinner back, not dessert. The adult's job is to let it happen and skip the lecture. "You're cold. Here's your coat," teaches more than five minutes of "I told you so." Natural consequences are not for danger. A child does not learn about the street by being hit by a car; the adult holds the hand.

When there is no safe natural consequence, use a *logical consequence*: something the adult sets up that is related to the behavior, respectful, and reasonable in size. Crayon on the wall means you help wash the wall. Throwing sand means you leave the sandbox for the rest of the visit. Riding the bike into the street means the bike is put away until tomorrow. The link is what makes it teaching instead of punishment. Losing screen time for a week because of crayon on the wall is unrelated and too big; a four-year-old cannot connect them, so she learns only that the adult is unpredictable.

Two more tools. Ignore what is only annoying: whining, a tantrum in a safe place, a rude word said for effect. Attention feeds behavior, and behavior that gets nothing tends to fade. And catch the child being good, specifically: "You put the cups on the table without being asked." Children repeat what gets noticed. An adult who notices five good things for every limit she sets will find she has to set far fewer limits.

words.d: moving a young child from something not allowed to something that is, by replacing the activity rather than just forbidding it
what happens by itself as a result of a child's choice, with nothing added by the adult; never used where there is danger
a result the adult sets up that is related to the behavior, respectful and reasonable in size

Buy him a new bike so he is not upset

No television for the weekend
A ten-minute time-out in the car
Leaving the sandbox for the rest of the visit

Explain that the cat has feelings and could be hurt
A time-out chair for one minute

lessons.title: Safe Sleep
lessons.mainIdea: Every sleep, every time: on the back, on a firm flat surface, alone in the sleep space with nothing else in it.
reading: It is 7:30 p.m. Kofi has finished his bottle and his eyes are closing. Dani carries him to the crib. What she sees should be this: a firm mattress that does not sink under his weight, a fitted sheet pulled tight, and nothing else. No blanket, no pillow, no stuffed animal, no bumper pads around the rails. She lays him down on his *back*, not his side, not his stomach, zipped into a wearable blanket called a sleep sack, and she leaves. That is *safe sleep*, and it is the same every nap and every night until he is one year old.

The reason is *SIDS*, sudden infant death syndrome, and suffocation. In the early 1990s, doctors found that babies put to sleep on their stomachs died in their sleep far more often than babies on their backs. The "Back to Sleep" campaign that followed cut those deaths roughly in half. Soft bedding is the other killer: a baby who rolls face-first into a pillow or a blanket cannot lift her head away. The crib looks bare to an adult. To a baby it is the safest place in the house.

The rest of the rules, from the American Academy of Pediatrics: room-share, not bed-share. The crib or bassinet goes in the parents' room for at least the first six months, but the baby never sleeps in an adult bed, on a couch or in an armchair with an adult; a sleeping adult can roll onto or against a baby. Keep the room a comfortable temperature and do not overdress; a baby who is sweating is too hot. No smoking in the home. Offer a pacifier at sleep time once breastfeeding is settled. Car seats, swings and bouncers are for travel and play, not for sleep; move a baby who falls asleep in one to a flat surface.

A baby who can roll over on his own may end up on his stomach, and that is all right; you still put him down on his back. Grandparents and older relatives often learned different rules, stomach sleeping, a blanket, a bumper to keep arms from getting stuck. The rules changed because babies died. The babysitter's job is to follow the current rule every time, and a parent's job is to tell every caregiver the rule and check that they follow it.

words.d: an infant on the back, on a firm flat surface, alone in the sleep space, with nothing else in it, every sleep
sudden infant death syndrome, the unexplained death of a baby under one year during sleep; back sleeping greatly lowers the risk
the baby sleeps in the parents' room in a separate crib or bassinet, not in the adult bed
a wearable blanket that zips around a baby so no loose blanket is needed in the crib

check.q: A tired parent falls asleep on the couch holding the baby. Why is this dangerous?

Prop him on his side with a rolled towel so he cannot roll
Put him in a swing where he cannot roll
Leave him; a baby who rolls on his own may stay that way, but he is still always put down on his back
